title: Why I Haven't Really Talked About AI This School Year
author: Marcus Luther
summary: High school English teacher Marcus Luther admits that after a summer spent speaking about talking with students on AI, he has hardly raised the topic in his own classroom seven weeks into the year. He lists three expected reasons: he resists AI tools for learning, his classroom is mostly analog, and his priority is building community before the harder conversations. He then names three less expected ones: agentic AI has left him feeling sidelined, he does not want to critique colleagues, and he is simply worried about AI overall and finds positive classroom uses an existential gaslighting. He argues this is not a failure, since he still brings AI up when it matters, through a study on homework reliance, Frankenstein, and a February research unit on critical AI literacy. His position is that he will design backward from what is good for students, not from the claim that AI is inevitable.
points: Luther's silence on AI follows from his own choices: no student-facing AI tools, no teacher AI use, and a mostly analog, screens-closed classroom.
Agentic AI has changed the conversation faster than many teachers can follow, and the barrier to joining it can feel intimidating.
He avoids judging colleagues because each teacher only knows his or her own context, and many have been left under-resourced on AI guidance.
AI is raised only when the curriculum calls for it, through research on homework reliance, Frankenstein and a February unit on critical AI literacy.
His stance is to plan backward from what is good for students, rather than from the argument that AI is inevitable.
quotes: I continue to resist any AI tools for learning. If I was being more proactive about experimenting with student-facing AI tools in the classroom or utilizing AI for my own work as a teacher, then I believe conversations around AI with students would have to take place early and often.
Most days, the answer is no—as I continue to love our spiral notebook system and the discussions that can thrive when all screens are closed and away.
When “talking about AI in education” mainly consisted of different forms of LLM chatbots, I felt adequate to the task.

At the same time, one of my longstanding instincts is the humility to acknowledge that the only context I really have any expertise in is my own classroom and to trust that other teachers are taking stock of their own contexts before making the best choices they can for their own students.

The scale of alarming feels increasingly monumental and essentially gets shoulder shrugged by proponents of AI in education, so forgive me if I’m not that motivated to try and find new AI tricks for my own practice.

I like that my classroom continues to be a place where students are not expected to use AI at the same time that it continues to be a place where they do not experience a teacher using AI. I think that’s important.

What I’m not going to do, though, is work backwards from AI in how I design my classroom. What I’m not going to do, though, is set aside my values and instincts as an educator (and human) in charting the path forward.
